content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) has established air quality guidelines to address indoor air pollution, with specific recommendations for reducing emissions from household fuel combustion. These guidelines are based on evidence from laboratory and field testing of fuel and technology combinations, as well as emissions modeling. 2. Laboratory testing provided moderate-quality evidence regarding emissions from various fuel and technology combinations, while field testing yielded low-quality evidence. This highlights the need for further research to validate findings in real-world settings. 3. Emission rate targets (ERTs) have been set to meet WHO 24-hour air quality guidelines for carbon monoxide (CO). These targets aim to ensure that a significant percentage of kitchens meet safe air quality levels. 4. Governments and implementing partners are strongly encouraged to develop strategies to accelerate the transition to low-emission technologies and fuels. This includes increasing access to and sustained use of clean fuels as rapidly as feasible. 5. Evidence suggests that some vented stoves (chimney stoves) can achieve indoor air pollution levels close to WHO interim targets (IT-1), ranging between 40–60 µg/m³. These findings provide a benchmark for evaluating the performance of various technologies and fuels in real-world conditions. 6. Systematic reviews have demonstrated a relationship between exposure to household air pollution (HAP) and the risk of acute lower respiratory infections in children. This evidence can guide assessments of the health benefits of interventions aimed at reducing HAP. 7. Technologies and fuels under consideration for promotion should undergo emissions testing, and where possible, actual air pollution levels in homes should be measured during everyday use. 8. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of developing tools and guidance to assess optimal interventions for reducing household air pollution. These tools should consider both health and environmental impacts. 9. The use of unprocessed coal as a household fuel is strongly discouraged due to its carcinogenic emissions, toxic contaminants (e.g., fluorine, arsenic, lead, selenium, mercury), and technical challenges in achieving clean combustion. 10. The household use of kerosene is also discouraged, as it poses risks of burns, fires, and poisoning, particularly in developing countries. Additionally, emissions from kerosene combustion may exceed air quality guideline levels for pollutants such as CO, nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and sulfur dioxide (SO₂). 11. The guidelines recommend that governments and agencies consider the health and climate co-benefits of household energy policies. This includes integrating household energy considerations into broader climate change mitigation strategies. 12. Implementation of these guidelines is particularly critical in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), where the health burden from household fuel combustion is greatest. Coordinated efforts involving national stakeholders, NGOs, and international organizations are essential to address these challenges. 13. WHO will provide technical support to selected countries to facilitate the implementation of these guidelines, learn from initial experiences, and refine tools and recommendations based on real-world outcomes. 14. The guidelines will be updated periodically through web-based mechanisms to incorporate new evidence on air quality, emissions, and health risks. This includes the development of interactive models that allow users to input region-specific data for more accurate assessments. 15. The use of solid fuels for cooking and heating remains a significant global health risk, contributing to approximately 4 million premature deaths annually. Transitioning to clean, safe, and efficient household energy solutions is essential to reduce this burden and achieve broader societal and environmental benefits. 16. These guidelines are intended for public health policymakers and specialists working across energy, environment, and other sectors to develop and implement policies that mitigate the adverse health impacts of household fuel combustion. 17. WHO and its partners will continue to monitor progress, evaluate program impacts, and provide technical support to ensure the successful implementation of these recommendations.
